subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]
passage: I watch my neighbour's son, Aryan, most evenings on the landing. When his sister hides behind the door and pops out, he gives a quick smile that is gone in a second, then he looks away. When she rolls the ball back and forth with him, he smiles for a long time, kicking his legs. I can't know exactly what he feels, but he keeps asking for the ball game again.

qa.q: What game makes Aryan smile for a long time?
qa.a: Rolling the ball back and forth with his sister.

qa.q: What does Aryan's quick smile at the peekaboo most likely show?
qa.a: Most likely a flash of joy at the surprise that fades fast; it could also be simple surprise, since he looks away quickly. 🙂

qa.q: What could his sister do if she wants more long smiles?
qa.a: Keep playing the games he asks for again, like the ball game, and follow his lead.

qa.q: How might a visitor misread the quick smile?
qa.a: They might think he is bored, but short smiles are normal for toddlers and do not mean disinterest.

grounding: It shows a toddler's fleeting smile at a surprise and sustained smile in a favourite game.

subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]

qa.q: Which game made Mia beam and keep smiling?
qa.a: The bubble game she loves.

qa.q: Why did Mia's father worry on Monday?
qa.a: Her smile at peekaboo was only a flicker, so he thought she might be bored; he later saw it was just a quick burst of joy.

qa.q: What did the father do well?
qa.a: He watched her across several days and tried different games instead of deciding too fast.

qa.q: What might have happened if he had stopped playing peekaboo?
qa.a: Mia could have missed out on a game that still gave her quick joy, even if her smiles were short. 😊

grounding: It shows that a toddler's short smiles at surprises and long smiles in familiar games are both normal joy.

subtype: Sustained and fleeting smiles in play [Expressing]

subtype: Dropped jaw and open mouth [Expressing]

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]
passage: "Is the dragon coming back?" asked Lina, five, squeezing her eyes shut. "In a minute," said her mother. "Do you want my hand?" Lina grabbed it. "Tell me when it's gone." Her brother groaned, "It's not even scary." "It is for me," said Lina, eyes still shut. "Okay, it's gone," said her mother. Lina opened one eye, then both. "Can we pause next time?" qa.q: What did Lina ask her mother to do?
qa.a: She asked her mother to tell her when the dragon was gone.

qa.q: Why did Lina squeeze her eyes shut?
qa.a: She was most likely scared of the dragon and was controlling her fear; she might also have been bracing for a loud part. 😰

qa.q: How does Lina's brother see the scene?
qa.a: He thinks it is not scary, which shows the same scene can feel very different to different people.

grounding: It shows a child shutting her eyes to cope with fear during a film, supported by an adult.

qa.a: He pressed both hands over his eyes.

grounding: It illustrates a child covering his eyes to control fear, with an adult offering a hand.

subtype: Eyes shut against a scary scene [Regulating]

qa.q: What made Guddi shut her eyes and hide her face?
qa.a: Most likely fear when the tiger leapt out; she might also have been startled by the sudden noise. 😰

subtype: Nodding to say yes [Expressing]
passage: At the clinic waiting room, the nurse asked five-year-old Rohan, "Do you understand you'll get a small pinch, and then a sticker?" Rohan nodded quickly. His mother knelt. "Can you tell me what will happen?" Rohan whispered, "A sticker." The nurse smiled. "And a small pinch first." Rohan's eyes widened, and he held his mother's hand. "Okay," he said, and nodded again, slower this time.

qa.q: What would Rohan get after the pinch?
qa.a: A sticker.

qa.q: What did Rohan's first quick nod most likely mean?

qa.a: She checked his understanding with a question instead of trusting the nod.

qa.q: How might the nurse see Rohan's second, slower nod?

subtype: Nodding to say yes [Expressing]
passage: I am Tanya's older sister, and I noticed something on Sunday. Mom asked Tanya, who is four, "Will you tidy the blocks before lunch?" Tanya nodded while still building. qa.q: What did Tanya choose when asked the second time?

subtype: Squinting and narrowed eyes [Interpreting]

qa.q: What happened when the teacher closed the curtains?

qa.a: They check the context, like light and the board, before deciding someone is angry.

subtype: Averting gaze as avoidance or respect [Interpreting]

subtype: Opening arms to invite closeness [Regulating]
